634.o: A small peninsula country on the east of the Arabian Peninsula and a world-class gas exporter.

096.o: A small Islamic sultanate on northern Borneo, wealthy from oil and gas.
096.ec: Oil and natural gas make up most exports and government revenue. With that money, it collects almost no taxes from citizens. It aims to expand into petrochemicals in preparation for the day its resources run out.

231.o: The birthplace of coffee and an ancient African country never colonized.
231.ec: Coffee is its signature export, along with flowers and sesame. Ethiopian Airlines is considered Africa's largest airline. Landlocked, it relies on the port of Djibouti, and foreign-currency shortages and ongoing internal conflict weigh heavily.

558.ec: It sells coffee, beef, gold and garment assembly, and remittances from the United States are large. Political repression has drawn Western sanctions.

478.ec: Iron ore, gold and fish are the main exports. Offshore gas development has made it a gas exporter.

170.o: A northern South American country on both the Caribbean and the Pacific, famous for coffee and flowers.
170.ec: It sells crude oil, coal, coffee, flowers and gold. Services and start-ups are growing around Medellin and Bogota. Reducing its reliance on fossil-fuel exports is hotly debated.

728.o: One of the world's youngest countries, independent from Sudan since 2011.
728.ec: Crude oil is almost all its exports and revenue. It can export only through a pipeline across Sudan, so it was hit directly by Sudan's civil war.

158.o: An island in East Asia that leads the world in advanced chipmaking and has built a vibrant democracy.
158.ec: It dominates the world's most advanced chip contract manufacturing and is strong in servers, electronic parts and machinery. Chips are such a big share of exports that the economy moves with demand for AI.

858.o: A small country between Brazil and Argentina, winner of the first football World Cup.
858.ec: It sells beef, pulp, soybeans and dairy, and makes most of its electricity from renewables. Stable politics and institutions give it one of the higher incomes in South America.

388.o: The Caribbean island country of reggae and sprinting.
388.ec: Tourism, remittances, and bauxite and alumina, the raw materials for aluminum, are the main sources of income. It has steadily reduced what was once a heavy public debt.

454.o: 'The warm heart of Africa', home to Lake Malawi.
454.ec: Tobacco makes up most exports. Most people live from farming, and droughts are frequent.

480.o: An Indian Ocean island country and one of Africa's wealthiest democracies.
480.ec: It started with sugar farming and expanded into tourism, textiles and offshore finance. It is counted among Africa's high-income countries with stable institutions.

328.o: An English-speaking country in northern South America, mostly covered by rainforest.
328.ec: Since oil production began at offshore fields in 2019, it has become the world's fastest-growing economy. It also sells gold, rice and sugar. How to share the oil money is the big challenge.

324.o: West Africa's 'water tower', where the Niger and Senegal rivers begin.
324.ec: It has the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the raw material for aluminum. Development of Simandou, one of the world's largest iron ore deposits, has begun and is expected to boost exports sharply.

108.o: A small landlocked country at the northern tip of Lake Tanganyika.
108.ec: Most people live from farming, and coffee and tea are the main exports. One of the poorest countries in the world, it is always short of foreign currency.

760.ec: Long civil war destroyed the economy. Since the change of government in 2024, sanctions relief and reconstruction investment have begun.

064.ec: Its biggest income is selling hydropower from dammed rivers to India. It charges tourists a high daily fee, earning a lot from relatively few visitors.

192.o: The largest island country in the Caribbean, known for music and baseball.
192.ec: The state runs most of the economy. Tourism, nickel, tobacco and doctors sent abroad are its main sources of foreign currency. Long-standing US sanctions, power shortages and scarce goods make the economy difficult.

104.ec: It sells natural gas, rice, clothing, gems and rare earths. The 2021 coup and civil war have shrunk the economy sharply and weakened the currency.

524.ec: Money sent home by people working abroad is a large part of the economy. Himalayan tourism and hydropower are its growth industries.

600.o: A landlocked country between Brazil and Argentina where Guarani and Spanish are both spoken.
600.ec: It sells soybeans and beef, and electricity from giant hydropower plants to Brazil and Argentina. Taxes are on the low side.

548.o: A South Pacific country of 83 islands.
548.ec: It sells tourism, copra, kava and beef, and also earns money through citizenship by investment.

258.ec: Tourism and black pearls are the two pillars. Tahitian black pearls farmed in island lagoons are the biggest export, along with tuna, vanilla and coconut oil. France tested nuclear weapons on its atolls from 1966 to 1996, and French government spending is still a big part of the economy.
258.o: 118 islands in five archipelagos scattered across the middle of the South Pacific, known for Tahiti and Bora Bora.
258.st: It has its own assembly and government and decides most matters itself. France handles foreign affairs, defense, justice and currency.

540.ec: It holds a large share of the world's nickel, and nickel ore and refined products make up most exports. As prices fell under pressure from Indonesian nickel for EV batteries, smelters closed or halted. Major unrest over a 2024 electoral reform badly shook the economy.
540.o: A large South Pacific island east of Australia, home to the Indigenous Kanak and people of European descent.
540.st: Under the Noumea Accord it has a special status with wide self-government. In three independence referendums since 2018, voters chose to stay with France each time.

876.ec: Most people live by subsistence farming and fishing. With almost no export industry, the islands rely on French government support and money sent home by people working in New Caledonia.
876.o: Small islands between Fiji and Samoa, where traditional kings still lead village affairs.
876.st: Three traditional kingdoms survive alongside the French administration.

666.ec: The islands lived on cod fishing, but fishing shrank sharply in the 1990s as cod stocks fell and fishing zones were drawn with Canada. Today French government spending and public-sector jobs make up most of the economy.
666.o: Small islands south of Newfoundland, the last piece of France in North America.
666.st: French territory just off the coast of Canada.

663.ec: Tourism is almost the whole economy. Hurricane Irma destroyed most buildings in 2017, and rebuilding took years. Low-tax, duty-free shopping also draws visitors.
663.o: The northern half of a Caribbean island, with no border checks to the south.
663.st: One island split in two: the north is French, the south is Sint Maarten, part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

652.ec: Luxury hotels, villas and yacht tourism are the core of the economy. There is no income tax, and visitors spend so much that incomes are high despite the small population.
652.o: A small Caribbean island famous as a retreat for the world's wealthy.
652.st: It runs its own affairs with its own tax system. It was once Swedish.

630.ec: Pharmaceutical and medical-device plants give manufacturing a big share of the economy. After it defaulted on its debt in 2016, a board created by Congress oversaw its finances, and Hurricane Maria wrecked the power grid in 2017. Many young people move to the US mainland.
630.o: A Caribbean island: Spanish-speaking US territory.
630.st: Residents are US citizens but cannot vote in presidential elections and send only a non-voting delegate to Congress.

316.ec: Tourism and US military bases are the two pillars. Most tourists come from Korea and Japan. There are US Air Force and Navy bases, and building work for Marines moving from Okinawa props up the economy.
316.o: The largest of the Mariana Islands in the western Pacific, a resort close to Korea and Japan.
316.st: Residents are US citizens but cannot vote in presidential elections.

850.ec: Cruise ships and resort tourism are the core of the economy. A big refinery on St. Croix has closed and reopened repeatedly, unsettling jobs.
850.o: Islands in the eastern Caribbean. As US territory, mainland visitors need no passport.
850.st: The United States bought the islands from Denmark in 1917.

016.ec: A tuna cannery is the biggest private employer and almost all exports. The rest depends on US government support and public-sector jobs.
016.o: The eastern islands of the Samoan archipelago in the South Pacific, where the traditional village system remains strong.
016.st: Residents are classed as US nationals, not US citizens.

580.ec: Tourism is the core of the economy, with visitors mainly from Korea. Garment factories once boomed but closed in the 2000s. The economy struggled after a casino resort project faltered.
580.o: Islands north of Guam. Saipan is the largest and popular with Korean tourists.
580.st: It became a US commonwealth under a covenant with the United States, and residents are US citizens.

060.ec: A world center of reinsurance: companies that share out insurers' losses after major disasters cluster here. Tourism is also big, and income per person is among the highest in the world.
060.o: An Atlantic island east of the United States, the oldest British Overseas Territory.
060.st: It runs its own government; the UK handles foreign affairs and defense.

136.ec: With no income or corporate tax, a large share of the world's hedge funds are incorporated here. Financial services and high-end tourism are the two pillars. Criticized as a tax haven, it has disclosed more information to meet international standards.
136.o: Three Caribbean islands northwest of Jamaica, famous as an offshore finance center.
136.st: It runs its own government; the UK handles foreign affairs and defense.

092.ec: Hundreds of thousands of shell companies set up by businesses worldwide are registered here, and their fees are a large share of government revenue. Yacht tourism is the second pillar.
092.o: Islands in the eastern Caribbean, known for yachting and for company registrations.
092.st: It runs its own government; the UK handles foreign affairs and defense.

796.ec: High-end beach tourism is most of the economy, with some offshore finance and seafood such as conch.
796.o: Islands southeast of the Bahamas, famous for white-sand beaches.
796.st: It runs its own government; the UK handles foreign affairs and defense.

660.ec: Upscale tourism was long the pillar, but the AI boom sent registrations of the island's internet domain, '.ai', soaring, and that income is now a large share of government revenue.
660.o: A small eastern Caribbean island known for beaches and luxury resorts.
660.st: It runs its own government; the UK handles foreign affairs and defense.

500.ec: The eruption buried the capital and airport, and more than half the people left. British government support now holds up the economy, with a little volcano tourism and volcanic sand mining.
500.o: A volcanic Caribbean island. A 1995 eruption turned its south into an exclusion zone.
500.st: It runs its own government but relies heavily on British support.

654.ec: Until an airport opened in 2016 it could be reached only by ship. British government support covers most of its budget, with a little high-priced island coffee, fishing and tourism.
654.o: A remote island in the middle of the South Atlantic, where Napoleon died in exile.
654.st: It forms one territory with Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.

612.ec: With only a few dozen residents, it lives on stamps, honey, handicrafts and British support. The surrounding sea is one of the largest marine reserves in the world.
612.o: A remote South Pacific island, home to descendants of the 18th-century Bounty mutineers.
612.st: One of the least populated inhabited territories in the world.

832.ec: Financial services such as funds, trusts and banking make up nearly half the economy. Jersey cattle, new potatoes and tourism are also well known.
832.o: An island in the English Channel between Britain and France, closer to the French coast.
832.st: A dependency of the British Crown, part of neither the UK nor the EU. It sets its own taxes and laws.

831.ec: Finance, such as captive insurers set up by companies to carry their own risks and fund administration, is the core of the economy. Income tax is low and there is no VAT.
831.o: An island in the English Channel that, with smaller neighboring islands, forms the Bailiwick of Guernsey.
831.st: A dependency of the British Crown, part of neither the UK nor the EU. It sets its own taxes and laws.

833.ec: Insurance, finance, online gaming and gambling drive the economy, drawn by low corporate tax.
833.o: An island in the Irish Sea between Britain and Ireland, famous for motorcycle races on public roads.
833.st: A dependency of the British Crown whose parliament, more than a thousand years old, sets its own laws and taxes.

248.ec: Shipping has long been the pillar. An exemption from EU tax rules lets ferries between Sweden and Finland stop here and sell duty-free goods, which has built up both shipping and tourism.
248.o: About 6,500 islands in the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland.
248.st: Part of Finland but an autonomous region where Swedish is the only official language, and demilitarized under international agreements.

574.ec: Tourism is the core of the economy. Since self-government ended, Australian taxes and welfare apply.
574.o: A small island between Australia and New Zealand, settled by descendants of the Bounty mutineers.
574.st: It long had its own assembly, but Australia took back self-government in 2016 and now runs it directly.

w: Transshipment makes up 60% of Busan's Q3 container traffic, up 20% from a year earlier
344.ec: A financial center with one of the world's top stock markets, banks and wealth management. It is the gateway through which Chinese companies raise money from foreign investors. Its port, re-export trade and logistics are also big. The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar, so it follows US interest rates.
344.o: A city on China's southern coast and Asia's international financial center.
344.st: Since returning from Britain to China in 1997, it has kept its own laws, currency and customs under 'one country, two systems'. Beijing's control has tightened sharply since the 2020 national security law.

446.ec: Its casino revenue is among the highest in the world, and most government revenue comes from gaming taxes. It depends heavily on visitors from mainland China, and Beijing is pressing it to diversify into tourism, conventions and finance.
446.o: A small city at the mouth of the Pearl River across from Hong Kong, where Portuguese buildings sit among casinos.
446.st: Since returning from Portugal to China in 1999, it has kept its own laws and currency under 'one country, two systems'.

010.ec: Since the 1991 Madrid Protocol, all mineral mining in Antarctica is banned except for research. Coal, iron ore and copper, and oil and gas in the surrounding seas, are thought to exist but cannot be developed. Most of the Earth's fresh water is locked in its ice. Economic activity today is almost entirely krill and toothfish fishing and Antarctic tourism, with catches set and managed under international agreements. Instead, many countries run bases to study climate, glaciers, space and life; Korea operates the King Sejong and Jang Bogo stations.
010.o: The icy continent at the southern end of the Earth. It belongs to no country.
010.st: Under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, no country can make new territorial claims, and the claims made by seven countries are frozen. Military activity is banned; only peaceful research is allowed.

254.ec: The Guiana Space Centre at Kourou is the pillar of the economy: being near the equator makes it ideal for rocket launches, and Europe's Ariane rockets lift off here. There is gold mining, but illegal mining in the forest is a big problem. Prices are higher and unemployment higher than on the mainland, and in 2017 mass protests brought the territory to a standstill.
254.o: Land in northeastern South America between Brazil and Suriname, mostly Amazon rainforest.
254.st: A region of France and part of the EU, under the same laws as mainland France. It is the only part of the EU on the South American continent.

312.ec: Bananas, sugarcane, rum and tourism are the main industries. Public-sector jobs and French government spending are a big share, and with so many imports, prices are higher than on the mainland. In 2009 a general strike over living costs shut the island down for more than 40 days.
312.o: Two butterfly-shaped islands joined together in the eastern Caribbean, plus smaller islands around them.
312.st: A region of France and part of the EU, under the same laws as mainland France.

474.ec: Bananas, rum made from sugarcane and tourism are the main industries. Its rum, distilled straight from cane juice, has a French protected designation of origin. Chlordecone, a pesticide long sprayed on banana plantations, contaminated soil and water and became a major social issue, and in 2024 big protests broke out over high food prices.
474.o: A volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean. The 1902 eruption of Mount Pelee wiped out its old main city.
474.st: A region of France and part of the EU, under the same laws as mainland France.

638.ec: Sugarcane, sugar, rum and tourism are the main industries. It is the largest and most developed French territory in the Indian Ocean, but unemployment is two to three times the mainland rate. French public spending and social security support household incomes heavily.
638.o: A volcanic island in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, home to the still very active Piton de la Fournaise.
638.st: A region of France and part of the EU, under the same laws as mainland France.

175.ec: The poorest region of France. Most jobs are in the public sector, with small sales of crops such as vanilla and ylang-ylang. Many people arrive from poorer Comoros, leaving housing and schools short, and Cyclone Chido devastated the island in 2024.
175.o: An island in the Mozambique Channel, southeast of the Comoros. Most residents are Muslim.
175.st: It became a French overseas department in 2011. Neighboring Comoros claims it.

744.ec: Coal mining was long the pillar, and Russia has run a mining town there under the treaty. Norway is closing its mines and shifting to tourism and Arctic research. Many countries' research stations cluster at Ny-Alesund, including Korea's Dasan Station. The Global Seed Vault, which stores seeds from around the world, is also here. Taxes are lower than on the Norwegian mainland.
744.o: Islands between Norway and the North Pole, the northernmost inhabited place in the world.
744.st: The 1920 Svalbard Treaty made it Norwegian, but citizens of treaty countries can live, work and do business there without a visa. Military bases are not allowed.

535.ec: Bonaire lives on coral-reef diving tourism and salt made by evaporating seawater. Sint Eustatius has a large oil storage terminal. Though part of the Netherlands, the islands use the US dollar, not the euro.
535.o: Three Dutch islands scattered across the Caribbean. Bonaire is the largest.
535.st: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba have been special municipalities of the Netherlands since 2010.
